hints: Focus on what a cation intermediate tells you, loss of chloride as Cl- leaves a carbocation, so think SN1 chemistry here.
Work out what type of carbocation each chloroalkane would give by looking at the carbon holding the Cl, is it attached to 1, 2 or 3 other carbons?
Remember the stability order from inductive electron donation, then see which structure gives the most alkyl groups around the positive carbon.
walkthrough:
**Spot the Mechanism Clue**

The question mentions a cation intermediate. That is a big hint for SN1 nucleophilic substitution.

In the slow step the C-Cl bond breaks heterolytically:
$$\text{R-Cl} \rightarrow \text{R}^{+} + \text{Cl}^{-}$$

**Find the Carbocation From Each Isomer**

Remove Cl and put the + charge on that carbon. Then classify it as primary, secondary or tertiary.

$\text{1-chlorobutane: CH}_{3}\text{CH}_{2}\text{CH}_{2}\text{CH}_{2}^{+}$ is primary. $\text{2-chlorobutane: CH}_{3}\text{CH}^{+}\text{CH}_{2}\text{CH}_{3}$ is secondary. $\text{1-chloro-2-methylpropane: (CH}_{3})_{2}\text{CHCH}_{2}^{+}$ is primary. $\text{2-chloro-2-methylpropane: (CH}_{3})_{3}\text{C}^{+}$ is tertiary.

**Rank Stability by Alkyl Groups**

Alkyl groups push electron density toward the positive carbon by the positive inductive effect. More groups means more stabilisation.

Stability order is:
$$\text{tertiary} > \text{secondary} > \text{primary}$$
So the tertiary cation from 2-chloro-2-methylpropane is the most stable.

options.A: 1-chlorobutane gives CH3CH2CH2CH2+, a primary carbocation with only one alkyl group donating electrons. It is stabilised the least, so it is not the most stable.
options.B: 2-chlorobutane gives CH3CH+CH2CH3, a secondary carbocation with two alkyl groups. It is more stable than primary but less stable than a tertiary cation.
options.C: 1-chloro-2-methylpropane gives (CH3)2CHCH2+, which is still a primary carbocation despite the branched skeleton. The positive carbon is attached to only one other carbon, so it is poorly stabilised.
options.D: 2-chloro-2-methylpropane gives (CH3)3C+, a tertiary carbocation. The positive carbon is surrounded by three methyl groups which donate electron density by the inductive effect, making this the most stable intermediate.
